title: The Hardest Lessons for Startups to Learn: release early, ship constantly, fear the right things
summary: Paul Graham distills seven counterintuitive startup lessons he finds himself repeating to YC founders. The core themes: release a minimal v1 fast, keep shipping small improvements, obsess over users and conversion, fear other startups and self-inflicted wounds instead of big companies, stay determined but flexible, and never count on a deal until it closes.

principles.text: Release a minimal v1 fast, then improve it from user reactions. Startups die from being too slow, not too quick.
principles.quote: I've seen a lot of startups die because they were too slow to release stuff, and none because they were too quick.

principles.text: Keep pumping out small improvements every day or two. Constant improvement doubles as marketing and builds fanatical loyalty.
principles.quote: If you're the rare exception-- a company that actually listens-- you'll generate fanatical loyalty. You won't need to advertise, because your users will do it for you.

principles.text: Explain what you do in one or two sentences, put your best stuff on the front page, and show rather than tell.
principles.quote: A startup should be able to explain in one or two sentences exactly what it does.

principles.text: Measure conversion of casual visitors into users via growth rate. Decent growth wins in the end; if not, fix something.
principles.quote: If you have decent growth, you'll win in the end, no matter how obscure you are now. And if you don't, you need to fix something.

principles.text: Fear other startups and self-inflicted wounds (internal disputes, inertia, ignoring users), not big companies. Ignoring users is worst.
principles.quote: Way more startups hose themselves than get crushed by competitors. There are a lot of ways to do it, but the three main ones are internal disputes, inertia, and ignoring users.

principles.text: Assume deals won't happen and keep looking for alternatives. Your only leverage in a deal is genuinely not needing it.
principles.quote: The only way a startup can have any leverage in a deal is genuinely not to need it.
